passage: Teacher's note, Class 11 project week. Written by Lokesh Sir. Shankar stayed back today and told me what he had noticed in his group of five. Meenal and Zubin had done almost all the research and the slides, while the other three, Shankar included until last week, kept saying, "We'll do it tomorrow." He said, "Sir, nobody's name is on any part, so nobody's responsible. The two careful ones end up doing everything, and today Meenal snapped at all of us." He said he felt bad about his own part. I have changed the project sheet: each member now signs for a named section, and there is a short check-in every Thursday. Shankar asked to take the data section.

qa.q: How many students were in Shankar's group?
qa.a: Five.

qa.q: Why did Shankar feel bad when he spoke to Lokesh Sir?
qa.a: He felt guilty, having been one of the three putting work off until last week, so he felt partly responsible for Meenal and Zubin carrying the load.

qa.q: What did Lokesh Sir change, and why should it help?
qa.a: Each member now signs for a named section with a Thursday check-in, so everyone is accountable and the careful two no longer carry everything.

qa.q: What might Meenal's snapping reveal about how Meenal felt?
qa.a: Meenal likely felt resentful and worn out after doing most of the research and slides while others kept postponing.

grounding: A student recognises that with no one accountable in a group project, two careful members carry the work and grow resentful, and the teacher adds named roles.

passage: Thursday. I'm one of the four boys in our geography project group, and today I finally saw what's been going on. Chinmay and Esther have done everything: the map, the report, the model of the river. The rest of us "helped" by sending thumbs-up in the group chat. Today Esther stayed back till six gluing labels while Abel and Sunny went to play football. Nobody is in charge of anything, so nobody feels guilty. Chinmay didn't complain, but when Sunny said, "Great work, team!" he went very quiet and packed up without saying bye. I think he's fed up. Honestly, I would be. Tomorrow I'm taking the labels home and doing the river section myself. And I'm going to suggest we each put our name on one part. - Thomas

qa.q: Until what time did Esther stay back?
qa.a: Till six.

qa.q: What does Chinmay packing up without saying bye suggest he felt?
qa.a: He seemed fed up and resentful that Esther and he did everything while the others shared the credit.

qa.q: What two choices does Thomas make for tomorrow, and why do they matter?
qa.a: Taking the labels home and doing the river section, and suggesting each person names one part, so the load is shared and everyone is accountable.

qa.q: How might Esther feel hearing 'Great work, team!'?
qa.a: Esther may feel irritated, since the team credit covered work that Esther and Chinmay mostly did.

grounding: A boy notices that in his group, with nobody accountable, two careful members carry the project and start to resent it, and he decides to change his part.

passage: In the government school at Sironj, the Class 10 science project was to test water from four village hand pumps. Gopal, fifteen, was in the group of six. From the back bench he watched it happen week after week. Payal walked to the pumps with bottles after school. Vandana wrote up every result in her neat hand. The other four, Gopal among them, said, "Tell us what to do," and then went to the tea stall. Nobody had a named job, so nobody felt it was theirs. On Friday Vandana slammed the file on the desk. "We are not your servants." Payal did not say anything, but she did not smile all day. Gopal saw it then: the careful ones had carried everything, and now they were fed up.

qa.q: Who wrote up every result for the project?
qa.a: Vandana wrote up every result in her neat hand.

qa.q: What does Gopal realise on Friday, and how might it feel?
qa.a: Gopal likely feels uncomfortable and a little ashamed, seeing that the careful ones carried everything and that Gopal was one of those who went to the tea stall.

qa.q: What choice could Gopal make now that he has seen the problem?
qa.a: He could ask the group to give each person a named job, and take one of the pump visits or write-ups himself.

qa.q: How does Payal seem to feel by Friday, and what shows it?
qa.a: She seems quietly hurt and tired of carrying the work, because she stays silent and does not smile all day.

grounding: A teenage boy watches his group leave the project to two diligent girls and sees how having no named jobs leaves them carrying the load and resenting it.

passage: In their school in Porto Alegre, the science-fair team had five names on the sign-up sheet. Emil, sixteen, noticed who actually stayed after the bell. Priscila, every day, rewiring the little wind turbine. Tomás, cutting blades out of plastic bottles. The other three, Emil included, kept saying, "Message us if you need anything," and walked out. On Wednesday the turbine would not spin. Priscila stayed until the caretaker switched off the lights. The next morning Emil heard her tell Tomás, "If our names are on it, why is it only us?" Tomás only shrugged and rubbed his eyes, looking worn out. Emil thought about the sign-up sheet in his bag. Five names, but no one was down for any single job, so three of them could vanish and nobody would notice. Except those two.

qa.q: What were Priscila and Tomás making for the science fair?
qa.a: They were building a little wind turbine, with Priscila rewiring it and Tomás cutting blades out of plastic bottles.

qa.q: What was Priscila feeling when she spoke to Tomás the next morning?
qa.a: She was frustrated and resentful, asking why only the two of them did the work when all five names were on the project.

qa.q: What could Emil do with what he has noticed?
qa.a: He could suggest writing one job next to each name on the sheet and take on a real part of the turbine himself instead of just offering to help by message.

qa.q: How does the situation look from Tomás's side?
qa.a: He is worn out from doing the work while others leave, and his tired shrug suggests he has stopped expecting the others to help.

grounding: A teenage boy observes that when no one has a named job, two careful teammates carry the whole project and grow resentful.

passage: The biology project on water testing was due Friday, and Pankaj, fifteen, had been watching his group all week in the school lab. Bhupen and Lata stayed back every day, labelling bottles, recording results. The other three, including Pankaj, kept saying, "We'll do the chart tomorrow." On Thursday, Pankaj walked in late and saw Bhupen redoing a graph someone had promised and never made. Bhupen didn't look up. His jaw was tight. "Ask your friends why they have time for cricket," he said to no one. Lata said nothing, but her eyes were red. Pankaj felt a jolt of shame. Nobody had been given a job with their name on it; so the two careful ones had quietly done everything, and now they were angry. He picked up a marker. "Tell me which part is mine," he said.

qa.q: What was Bhupen redoing when Pankaj walked in?
qa.a: Bhupen was redoing a graph someone had promised and never made.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling when he saw Bhupen's tight jaw?
qa.a: Pankaj felt a jolt of shame, recognising that he and the others had left the work to the two careful members.

qa.q: What could the group do to avoid this in the next project?
qa.a: They could give each person a named job with a deadline at the start, so no one can free ride and the load is shared.

qa.q: How does Bhupen feel about carrying the work?
qa.a: Bhupen feels resentful and angry, as his remark about cricket and his tight jaw show.

grounding: A student sees classmates leave group work to two diligent members and recognises that without accountability the careful ones carry the load and resent it.

passage:
Dear Nazia didi,
You asked how the history project went. Honestly, I've been watching something that bothers me.
There are five of us. From the first week, Anu and Rafi did everything: the research, the model, even printing. The rest of us just added our names. Every time the class group chat had a question, Anu answered in ten minutes and the rest of us sent thumbs-up stickers.
Yesterday, at the practice presentation, Anu snapped. She said, "Do the three of you even know what our topic is?" Rafi didn't defend us. He just looked tired.
I realised no one was ever given a specific task, so it was easy to let the careful ones do it. And now they're angry, and they have a right to be. I'm going to ask Sir if we can split the next part by name.
Karthik

qa.q: How quickly did Anu answer questions on the group chat?
qa.a: Anu answered in ten minutes.

qa.q: What does Karthik seem to feel after the practice presentation?
qa.a: Karthik seems uncomfortable and guilty, recognising that the others were right to be angry.

qa.q: Why is splitting the next part by name a good idea?
qa.a: Clear, named tasks make everyone accountable, so the careful members don't end up carrying everything.

qa.q: How might Rafi feel after weeks of doing most of the work?
qa.a: Rafi seems exhausted and resentful, too tired even to defend the others.

grounding: A student sees the group leave the work to two diligent members, and recognises that without accountability they carry the load and grow resentful.

passage: Kunal, you asked why I went quiet in our group chat. Okay. I'm Abhinav, and in our chemistry project, I watched something happen and I didn't like what I saw in myself. Shreya and Farhan did everything. Every time a deadline came, they stayed up. The rest of us, me included, kept saying, "I'll do the conclusion," and never did. There was no list, no names next to tasks. So the two most careful people just picked up the slack. Last week Shreya sent a message: "Are the rest of you even part of this?" Farhan left the group chat for a day. I realised: when nobody is responsible, the responsible ones get crushed. They don't just get tired, they start resenting the whole team. So I messaged them and said I'll do the conclusion tonight, and I did.

qa.q: Which part did Abhinav finally do?
qa.a: Abhinav did the conclusion that night.

qa.q: What did Abhinav feel on seeing what was happening in the group?
qa.a: Abhinav felt uneasy and ashamed, not liking what that moment showed about Abhinav's own behaviour.

qa.q: What could the group do so that careful members aren't crushed next time?
qa.a: They could write a list with names next to tasks, making everyone accountable from the start.

qa.q: What was it like for Farhan to leave the group chat for a day?
qa.a: Farhan was likely fed up and resentful after carrying so much of the work.

grounding: A student observes classmates leaving project work to two diligent members, sees how lack of accountability breeds resentment, and takes on a fair part.

passage:
I'm Irfan, the boy who sits at the back of 10B and watches. In our science project group there were six of us. On paper.
In the first meeting, Ishita and a quiet boy from the front bench made a list. Everyone nodded. Then the four others, and honestly me too at first, just disappeared into cricket and phones.
By the second week I saw Ishita in the library at lunch every day, charts spread out, eating with one hand. The front-bench boy stayed late to finish the model.
On submission day, the four got the same marks. Ishita didn't say anything, but she didn't sit with us after that.

qa.q: How many people were in the science project group on paper?
qa.a: There were six of them on paper.

qa.q: What might Irfan be feeling as he watches Ishita eating with one hand in the library?
qa.a: He seems uneasy and a little guilty, noticing she is carrying the work while he and others slipped away.

qa.q: What could Irfan do next time the group shares out work?

qa.q: How does Ishita seem to see the group by the end?

grounding: Illustrates a male student noticing classmates leave group work to two diligent members, who carry the load and grow resentful when no one is held accountable.

passage:
Dilnaz, you complain about your group project? Listen to your Nana. I'm Yash, and in 1978 I was fifteen and in a group of seven boys making a model of a dam for the district fair.
Two of them, the headmaster's nephew and a thin boy from the mill colony, did everything. The rest of us brought snacks and opinions. I watched them glue matchsticks until midnight, and I told myself they enjoyed it.
The day before the fair, the thin boy threw the glue pot on the floor. "Do it yourselves," he said. He never came to our group again.
We won second prize. I remember his face more than the prize.

qa.q: How many boys were in the group making the dam model?
qa.a: There were seven boys in the group.

qa.q: What does Yash seem to feel when he says he remembers the boy's face more than the prize?
qa.a: He still feels regret and some shame, because he watched the two careful boys carry the load and told himself they did not mind.

qa.q: What could the boys have done differently when the work began?
qa.a: They could have divided the model into parts with one boy responsible for each, so the two careful boys were not left gluing alone until midnight.

qa.q: How did the thin boy from the mill colony feel when he threw the glue pot?
qa.a: He felt resentful and used, after doing the work while the others brought only snacks and opinions.

grounding: Shows a teenage boy, now an elder, recalling how two diligent group members carried the load until resentment made one of them quit.

passage: The biology project was due at nine the next morning, and a power cut had blacked out half of Jaipur. In the group chat, Binita and Farhan were still dividing slides by candlelight. At 2:15 Binita typed, 'I'm done carrying this group.' Eshaan felt a hot rush of shame. He opened the file and took the last three slides.

passage: In Class 11C at the Darjeeling school, the history project was a group of five, and by week three Tushar could see how it would go. He and Dolma had written the outline, made the timeline and booked the library. The other three had 'network issues' every evening and 'forgot' every Friday. At the Saturday meeting Dolma arrived with the printed charts, dark circles under her eyes, and snapped at a joke she would usually laugh at. Tushar understood. Nobody was checking who did what, so the careful two did everything, and the careful two were starting to hate the other three. He felt it too, a sour heat whenever Pranav said 'great work, guys'. That evening he made a simple table, each name, each task, a date, and sent it to the teacher and the group.

qa.q: What had Tushar and Dolma done by week three?
qa.a: Written the outline, made the timeline and booked the library.

qa.q: What did Tushar feel when Pranav said 'great work, guys'?
qa.a: Tushar felt a sour heat of resentment, knowing Pranav had done almost nothing.

qa.q: Why is Tushar's table a good step?
qa.a: It makes each person's task visible and accountable, so the work is shared and resentment has less room to grow.

qa.q: Why did Dolma snap at a joke she would usually laugh at?
qa.a: Dolma was exhausted and resentful after carrying most of the project, so her patience had worn thin.

grounding: A teenage boy notices group work always falls to him and one other careful classmate, and the resentment it breeds.

passage:
'You're still up?' Yash asked, finding Tushar at the hostel desk at 1 am.
'The economics project. Due tomorrow.'
'Isn't it a group of six?'
'Yeah. Me and Nazia are doing it.'
'And the other four?'
'Karan said his laptop broke. Rhea said she'd do the graphs, then went to a wedding. The others said "just tell us what to present".'
'That's the third project like this.'
'I know.' Tushar rubbed his eyes. 'Every time. Me and Nazia. Same grade for all six.'
Yash watched him type. 'You sound angry.'
'I'm starting to hate them. I don't want to.'
'Then don't do it all again. Write down who does what and tell Sir before the next one. If nobody's accountable, you'll always be the one carrying it.'
Tushar paused, then opened a new file and typed: Task list.

qa.q: How many members are in Tushar's economics group?
qa.a: A group of six.

qa.q: What does Yash feel watching Tushar type at 1 am?
qa.a: Yash feels concerned for his friend, noticing the anger and exhaustion.

qa.q: What does Yash suggest, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Writing down who does what and telling Sir before the next project, so everyone is accountable and the careful few stop carrying it.

qa.q: How does Tushar feel about the other four?
qa.a: Tushar feels resentful and tired, starting to hate them for leaving the work again, though he doesn't want to.

grounding: A teenage boy sees his friend carry group projects while others free ride, and names the accountability gap.

passage: Looking back at last term's geography project, I think I saw it before anyone said it. There were six of us. Pema made the map. Rajni wrote the report and stayed after school to print it. The rest of us, me included for the first week, sent "nice!!" in the group chat and nothing else. Nobody had a named job, so nobody had to do anything. On the Thursday before submission, Rajni snapped at Pema over a missing legend, and Pema cried in the library. They weren't angry at each other. They were exhausted, and angry at us. That week I finally helped glue the charts, and Rajni muttered, "At least one of you showed up, Dorjee bhai." I felt like a fraud. For the next project, I asked for a list with each person's name next to a task.

qa.q: Who made the map?
qa.a: Pema.

qa.q: Why did Dorjee feel like a fraud?
qa.a: Dorjee felt ashamed, having sent only "nice!!" for a week while Pema and Rajni carried the load, and then being thanked for gluing a few charts.

qa.q: What did Dorjee change for the next project, and why does it help?
qa.a: Dorjee asked for a list with each person's name next to a task, so everyone is accountable and the careful few don't carry it all.

qa.q: How did Pema and Rajni feel by the Thursday before submission?
qa.a: They were exhausted and angry at the rest of the group, which came out as snapping and crying.

grounding: A student sees classmates leave a group project to the same two careful members, who end up carrying the load and resenting it.
